Empirical Research Plan  
“How does the availability of student aid influence college attendance and completion rates?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Two–way‐fixed‐effects Difference-in-Differences (DiD), supplemented by a 2-stage-least-squares (2SLS) “Wald-type” DiD to translate policy-driven eligibility into dollars actually received.

Why DiD?  
• We observe explicit policy variation that (i) begins in a known year, (ii) applies only in a subset of U.S. states (or to cohorts defined by HS-graduation year), and (iii) is plausibly exogenous to individual college decisions.  
• NLSY follows the same people annually, so we can difference out permanent student-level unobservables with individual fixed effects and sweep out common shocks with year fixed effects.  
• IPEDS supplies state-year controls for higher-ed supply conditions, improving precision.

2SLS extension  
Stage 1: instrument “aid dollars received” with “Post t × Treated s” eligibility to recover the causal response to an extra $1,000 of aid, not just the intent-to-treat (ITT).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated_is = 1 if student i’s state (or cohort) s is covered by the new rule AND calendar year t ≥ policy start year for that state/cohort.

Control group  
Students in never-treated or not-yet-treated states/cohorts observed in the same calendar years.

Timing / key variation  
Policy start year differs across states (or cohorts), generating staggered timing. The basic DiD term is:

PostPolicy_st × Eligible_s

where PostPolicy_st = 1 in all years t ≥ implementation in state/cohort s.

Outcome variables  
(1) Enroll_it = 1 if enrolled in any accredited post-secondary institution that year.  
(2) Complete_it = 1 if i has earned a Bachelor’s (or AA) by year t.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel pre-trends: In the absence of the policy, treated and control units would have evolved similarly.  
Plausibility: Many states see similar secular trends in college-going; we will test with event-study graphs.

A2. No differential anticipation: Students could not pre-shift enrollment in response to knowledge of the reform.  
Plausibility: Aid rules were finalized close to implementation; HS seniors had at most a few months’ notice.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers): An individual’s outcome is unaffected by others’ eligibility status.  
Reasonable because financial aid is federally funded and not rationed at the margin.

A4. Policy exogeneity conditional on controls: States did not time or design aid changes in response to unobserved shocks to college going.  
Plausibility heightened if the reform was federal but phased-in via administrative capacity, not demand.

A5. First stage relevance (for 2SLS): The policy materially shifts aid dollars.  
Checkable in data.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-policy trends  
• Mitigation: Plot event-study coefficients for −6 … −1 leads; include state×linear-time trends; drop states failing pre-trend F-test.

T2. Concurrent policies (e.g., tuition caps, merit scholarships)  
• Mitigation: Control for other state-year higher-ed policies drawn from SHEEO or IPEDS; include state×year covariates such as tuition, unemployment, and per-capita income.

T3. Selective migration / residency requirement gaming  
• Mitigation: Restrict sample to individuals observed in the same state during high-school years; re-estimate on non-movers; show results unchanged.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#############################
# 1. Load packages
#############################
library(readr)       # data import
library(dplyr)       # data wrangling
library(fixest)      # fast FE regressions & 2SLS
library(ggplot2)     # graphs

#############################
# 2. Import & merge data
#############################
nlsy   <- read_csv("NLSY_individual_panel.csv")
ipeds  <- read_csv("IPEDS_state_year.csv")

df <- nlsy %>%
      left_join(ipeds, by = c("state","year"))

#############################
# 3. Construct variables
#############################
df <- df %>%
  mutate(post     = ifelse(year >= policy_year_state, 1, 0),
         treated  = ifelse(state_treated == 1, 1, 0),
         did      = post * treated,
         enroll   = as.numeric(enrolled_any_college),
         complete = as.numeric(degree_ba_aa),
         aid_usd  = aid_received,
         # controls
         age      = year - birth_year,
         female   = (sex == "F"),
         black    = (race == "Black"),
         hisp     = (race == "Hispanic"))

#############################
# 4. Main ITT DiD (Enroll)
#############################
itt_enroll <- feols(enroll ~ did + age + female + black + hisp |
                          id + year,
                    data = df, cluster = ~state)
summary(itt_enroll)

#############################
# 5. 2SLS: Aid dollars effect
#############################
iv_enroll <- feols(enroll ~ 1 | id + year | aid_usd ~ did,
                   data = df, cluster = ~state)
summary(iv_enroll)

#############################
# 6. Event-study (pre-trend test)
#############################
df <- df %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  mutate(rel_year = year - policy_year_state) %>%
  ungroup()

es_model <- feols(enroll ~ sunab(rel_year, treated) + age + female + black + hisp |
                         id + year,
                  data = df, cluster = ~state)
iplot(es_model)

#############################
# 7. Robustness: drop movers
#############################
df_nomove <- df %>% filter(moved_state == 0)

itt_nomove <- feols(enroll ~ did + age + female + black + hisp |
                          id + year,
                    data = df_nomove, cluster = ~state)
summary(itt_nomove)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (credit-constraint models) predicts aid ↑ → enrollment and persistence ↑.  
Magnitude priors (per $1,000 in additional grant aid):  
• College entry +3–4 percentage points for low-income youths (≈ 10 % uplift on a 35 % baseline).  
• BA completion +2 pp within 6 years.  
Overall ITT (eligibility dummy) should therefore be smaller but positive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Relevant first stage (eligibility → aid)......................1  
2. No manipulation of assignment (eligibility predetermined)...1  
3. Parallel pre-trends (supported by event study)...............0.8  
4. No concurrent confounders unaccounted for....................0.7  
5. Stable composition & SUTVA...................................1  
Average score…………………………………………………………0.9

I judge the design to be strong but will devote particular attention to validating parallel trends and ruling out coincident policy shocks.
